Then, in order to fulfill former vows, for the sake of setting the wheel of Dharma in motion, and for the arising of the Blessed One, one should look upon the infinite realm of space. Just as before, with the four mandalas of wind and so forth, one should visualize a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāṅgāra*) in the center upon a vajra ground. Therein, one should visualize the foundational mandala—which consists of the three wheels of mind, speech, and body—as a square transformed from the syllable *cuṃ* or the syllable *oṃ*. Within that, the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*) is surrounded by three enclosures of black, red, and white, has four gates, is multicolored, and is adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*).

The outer terrace is adorned with jeweled necklaces (*ratnāvalī*), strings of pearls (*hāra*), half-strings (*ardhahāra*), *vakulī* ornaments, and *kūrmaśīrṣa* motifs; it is further embellished with moon-discs, banners, bells, chowries, mirrors, and so forth.

In its center, measuring half of that [outer terrace], is the Wisdom Wheel (*jñānacakra*), encircled by a garland of vajras and graced by sixteen pillars. Half of that again is the place of the Blessed One, adorned with a garland of vajras.
Having thus visualized the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*).

Twice that size is the Speech-wheel (*vākcakra*), likewise surrounded by five walls, twice the measure [of the previous], and similarly adorned with four gates, chowries, and so forth at the ends. Outside of that, twice its size is the Body-wheel (*kāyacakra*), likewise twice the measure, adorned with five walls, four gates, and so forth. Everywhere, the ground is black in the east and southeast, red in the south and southwest, yellow in the west and northwest, and white in the north and northeast. There are outer enclosures of earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as a vajra-fence and vajra-flames.

Having thus visualized the maṇḍala circle with the great cremation grounds situated within the wind-rim, one should contemplate the seats described in the verses of homage as being in their respective places for the deities.
Therein, one should meditate upon the twenty-four lotuses situated on the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) as transformations of the syllable *paṃ* together with moons;
however, the roots, stalks, petals, filaments, pericarps, and seeds of each individual lotus are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.
Likewise, other things are also briefly described therein: the bulb and stalk of the lotuses arise from the syllable *ka*; the petals and stamens are produced from the syllable *u*;
the central pericarp contains the moon-seat from the syllable *aṃ* and the sun-seat from the syllable *raṃ*.

Then, in the twenty-fifth [petal], the central lotus, one should mentally meditate upon a quartet of mandalas—moon, sun, Rāhu, and fire—arising from the transformation of the syllable *paṃ*. Therein, one should visualize oneself as the Lord Kālacakra, endowed with the characteristics described in the verses of salutation, perfected through the five wisdoms such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) as taught in the *Vajravega-samādhi*, and embraced by Viśvamātā whose characteristics are likewise stated there. One should then behold the eight goddesses beginning with Kṛṣṇadīptā and the four emblems beginning with the jewel.
This is the generation of Vajrasattva.

Then, having caused the assembly of Jinas such as Akṣobhya to enter one's own body by means of the sound of sexual union (*suratadhvani*), and having manifested the assembly of the elements such as space in the form of deities—consisting of the male consort, the wisdom-consort, the eyes, and so forth, as well as the objects of the senses such as form—one should again emit that [assembly] from one's own body and properly cause it to be absorbed into Viśvamātṛ.

Then, having likewise emitted them once more as Tathāgatas in the form of a maṇḍala-circle, together with their relics, one should cause them to enter one’s own body; having caused them to become liquid moon-like and emitted them through one’s own vajra, one should meditate upon the maṇḍala of the assembly of male and female deities—which has been transformed therein and is characterized by the relationship of support and supported—with Akṣobhya as the presiding lord within the interior of the lotus of one’s own vidyā, and then cause it to enter the body of the Blessed One as before.
Then, having meditated upon the deities of the maṇḍala possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, one should seat them in their respective places.
Thereafter, one should assume the ego-identity: "I am of the nature of the wisdom of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu."
Then, out of compassion, one should consecrate all sentient beings;

and likewise, having meditated there upon the Blessed One Kālacakra—who consists of the five gnoses and is crowned by Vajrasattva—this is the procedure for the sādhana of the Blessed Śrī Kālacakra, whose nature is the utterly pure dharmadhātu.

Then, having drawn in all sentient beings belonging to the six realms of existence and visualized them as having entered that very maṇḍala, one should cause Vairocana and the other Tathāgatas to enter one’s own heart; having caused them to become the nature of reality (*sadhabhūta*) and melted into the essence of bodhicitta, one should emit them by means of one’s own secret vajra. One should then meditate upon those all sentient beings as being consecrated by that bodhicitta.

Furthermore, one should visualize all those sentient beings touched by the rays of bodhicitta as having three faces, various colors, possessing the forms of deities, consisting of wisdom and method, and filled with the bliss of supreme joy.
Then, one should instantly perceive their own bodies as having become the nature of the maṇḍala wheel;
therein are the seed-syllables of the mantras, joined with various consonants and accompanied by vowels.

Here, the collection of all consonants is the letter *kṣa*; by that indicator, whichever is the first name of anyone, its corresponding consonant is used, and by means of that, all of it should be performed.
Here, *kṣa kṣi kṣu kṣū kṣlṛ* are the five Tathāgatas beginning with Vajra-jñāna; likewise, *kṣā kṣī kṣṛ kṣū kṣlṛ* are the five elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Similarly, *kṣa kṣa kṣa kṣa kṣa kṣaṃ* are the six Bodhisattvas beginning with Śruti (the ear);
likewise, *kṣā kṣai kṣār kṣau kṣāl kṣāḥ* are the six sense objects.
Likewise, *kṣlṛ*, *kṣyā*, *kṣā*, *kṣvā*, and *kṣlā* are the five organs of action (*karmendriya*);
likewise, *krodhaḥ*, *kṣlṛ*, *kṣyā*, *kṣā*, *kṣvā*, and *kṣlā* are the objects of the five organs of action.
Thus, there are the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five organs of action, and the five objects of the organs of action.

Thus, having instantaneously produced all sentient beings as possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and having the form of a mandala-circle, and having bestowed consecration upon all sentient beings out of compassion, one should cause them to enter their respective fields;
this is the "Arising of the Body," the *maṇḍalarājāgrī-samādhi*, which is the limb of service (*sevā*).
Then, one should meditate on the descent [of the deity] in that manner, and likewise it is said therein: "The syllable *hoḥ* at the navel and at the crown of the head."

Between these two, the body-vajra *Oṃ* is interwoven on the forehead; the speech-vajra *Āḥ* at the throat; and the mind-vajra *Hūṃ*, the three syllables characterized by body, speech, and mind, at the heart.
Then they further say:
"By the rays of the *Hoḥ*-syllable of gnosis at the navel, the body, speech, and mind vajras are melted into the lotus of equal bliss; melted by the passion of wisdom, that Lord is like the moon."
Then, Tārā and the others urge the Blessed One, who has swiftly entered [the state of union] together with Prajñā;
thus, Tārā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Locanā— whose natures are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— sing this song,
as it is stated in the Root Tantra:
Furthermore, there I am Locanā, the Mother of the World, abiding in the *niṣyanda* [result] for yogins by way of the nature of my maṇḍala; O Kālacakra, you who have arisen from desire, know me!
And I am the sister Māmakī, abiding in the *vipāka* [result] for yogins.
By my nature as the mandala, I am Kālacaja-born Desire; and Pāṇḍarā is my daughter, who abides within the man among yogins.
By my nature as the mandala, I am Kālacaja-born Desire; [I am] me.
I am Tāriṇī, the sister’s daughter, established in the stainlessness of yogins;
through the nature of my maṇḍala, O Kālacakra, arise with desire for me,
taking up the maṇḍala of emptiness, the maṇḍala of body, speech, and mind.
"O Lord of the World, expand yourself! O you whose intention is to uplift the world!

Then, having entered into emptiness there, the Blessed One, being awakened by these songs, perceives the entire world as like an illusion and again brings about rebirth for the sake of sentient beings.

Thereafter, in that same manner, having meditated upon Kālacakra—accomplished through the transformation of his own seed-syllable and emblem and crowned with Akṣobhya—one should perform the placement of the mudrās and so forth using the previously mentioned mantra-words, while omitting the elephant-hide, the mudrās, and the mantras for the placement of the nāgas.

Then one should place the inner mudrās there as follows: here, in the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra, at the drop (*bindu*), is Akṣobhya with the syllable *a*; likewise, in the heart, in the maṇḍala of Rāhu, is Amoghasiddhi with *i*;
and on the forehead, in the maṇḍala of the moon, is Amitābha with *u*—this is the Odd Family in the Odd Cakra.
Likewise, Vairocana at the navel in the *lṛ*-kāla-fire; Ratneśa at the throat in the sun;
and Vajrasattva at the secret place in the *aṃ*-jñāna-maṇḍala—this is the rule for the sealing (*mudraṇa*) of the deities. Furthermore, regarding the sealing of the body and the sealing of speech:
LṚ at the navel, Ū at the heart, Ṛ at the throat.
Ī should be placed on the forehead and Ā on the uṣṇīṣa within the mandalas of earth and the other elements;
likewise, for the sealing with the mind-bindu, OṂ is placed on the forehead within the moon-mandala.
Āḥ at the throat on the solar mandala;
Hūṃ at the heart on the Rāhu mandala; Hoḥ at the navel on the Kālāgni mandala.
Likewise, the sealing with gnosis (*jñānamudraṇa*) is the syllable *a*, because all phenomena are primordially unarisen;
thus, at the vajra-jewel, one attains the accomplishment (*siddhi*) through the syllable *a*.
Then, having recited "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the perfectly pure wisdom of the dharmadhātu," one should emanate the deities of the maṇḍala.

Through the meditative absorption of the union of wisdom and means, one causes the Buddhas—who abide in space as the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and who possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas for the sake of the pledge-maṇḍala—to enter one's own body. Then, within the lotus of wisdom, one should emanate [the deities] from the Blessed Lord Śrī Kālacakra’s ritual manual for accomplishment, whose nature consists of the individual syllables of the mantra.
As before, one should understand the characteristics of the faces, arms, emblems, and postures within the maṇḍalas of gnosis, mind, speech, and body.

Having thus performed the dismissal of the maṇḍala, one should meditate in the center of the heart-lotus, upon the pericarp, on a black five-pronged vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*, accompanied by moon, sun, and fire, and emitting five-colored rays. Having emanated Vajravega, who possesses the previously described characteristics and resides within the syllable *hrīḥ*, one should visualize a vajra-hook transformed from the syllable *jaḥ* in the center of the hub (*varaṭaka*) of that vajra.

And by means of the rays of that Vajrāṅkuśa, which have the form of a vajrāṅkuśa, one should attract the pure wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) that has arisen with the speed of a vajra and is perfected in the form of the three worlds;
then Vajravega returns to his own place,
and thereafter one should perform the entry and so forth with the four wrathful deities— Jambhaka, Stambhaka, Mānaka, and Atibala.

And so it is stated therein: "In this way, [the deities] are drawn in by the syllable *jaḥ*, made to enter by the syllable *hūṃ*, bound by the syllable *vaṃ*, gratified by the syllable *hoḥ*, and made of one flavor (*samarasīkṛta*) by the syllable *hīḥ*; [this is done] with the vajra-hook, the vajra, the vajra-noose, the vajra-bell, and the vajra-staff.

Having thus worshipped the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*), one should meditate on its becoming of one flavor with the commitment-wheel (*samayacakra*) as before; such is the rule. As for their mutual sealing (*mudraṇa*), it should be meditated upon according to the sequence stated in the verses of salutation. This is the completion of the forms of the deities.
Then, one should perform the consecration of the body and so forth.

And so, there, on the forehead, one should visualize a moon disc transformed from the syllable *A*; above that, an eight-spoked wheel transformed from the syllable *Oṃ*; and from that, the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), white in color, with three faces—the central face white, the left red, and the right black—with six arms. He holds a wheel, a vajra, and a lotus in his right hands, and a sword, a bell, and a jewel in his left hands. Having thus produced him together with his consort (*saprajña*), one should emanate him from the forehead and contemplate the entire realm of space as being completely filled by him. After he has performed the teaching of the Dharma for those beings who are to be disciplined by the Body-Vajra, he returns and stands before oneself; one should then entreat him for empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
"May the holders of the Body-Vajra consecrate me.
Then, the deities of the Body Family consecrate him with jars of nectar.
Once he has been consecrated, one should perform the empowerment of the blessing (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Having caused the Body-Vajra to enter the moon-maṇḍala on the forehead, one should utter this: "May the glorious Holder of the Body-Vajra, who is meditated upon as indivisible from the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment of the Body-Vajra."
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
bestow upon me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Body holders!
Thus concludes the empowerment of the body.

166. *Dhī*: Thus, at the throat, there is a sun-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *repha*; above that, an eight-petalled red lotus transformed from the syllable *ākāra*; and upon that, the Speech-Vajra (Vāgvajra) together with his consort, red in color, with faces that are red, white, and black. He holds a lotus, a vajra, and a wheel in his right hands, and a jewel, a bell, and a sword in his left hands. Having emanated him and visualized the expanse of space (*ākāśadhātu*) as completely filled by him, and having performed the teaching of the Dharma for those beings who are to be disciplined by the Speech-Vajra, one should again establish him in front of oneself and entreat him for empowerment, saying: "May the Speech-Vajra holders empower me!"

Then, having visualized oneself being consecrated by the speech-family goddesses with jars of nectar, one should perform the empowerment of speech (*vāgadhiṣṭhāna*). Having placed the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) within the solar mandala, one should utter this: "May the glorious Holder of the Speech-Vajra, who is meditated upon as inseparable from the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment of the Speech-Vajra."
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra of Speech!
Thus concludes the section on the presiding deity of speech.

In the heart, which is the locus of the mind, one should visualize within the orb of Rāhu a blue-colored drop; above that, a five-pronged vajra transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*; and from that, the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*) together with his consort, black in color, with faces that are black, red, and white. He holds a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in his right hands, and a bell, a jewel, and a sword in his left. Having emanated him, one should visualize the expanse of space as being completely filled by him. After he has performed the teaching of the Dharma for those beings who are to be disciplined by the Mind-Vajra, one should establish him once again before oneself and request the consecration.
"May all the deities of the Mind-Vajra family consecrate me.
Then, having visualized oneself being consecrated by the goddesses of the Mind-Vajra family, one should perform the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Having placed the Mind-Vajra within the mandala of Rāhu, one should utter this: "The glorious Holder of the Mind-Vajra is realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras."
May the Vajra-Mind of the Buddha bestow upon me today the state of empowerment.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O holders of the mind-vajra.

Having thus performed the empowerment of the mind (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*), the rule is that the yogi should maintain the ego-identification (*ahaṅkāra*) here as a unity, thinking: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.

In this way, for the Prajñā, there is the syllable *ho* at the navel; for the Blessed Śrī Kālacakra, the procedure for the sādhana is the syllable *svā* at the secret place; and for the Trikula Upāya, there is the syllable *hā* at the uṣṇīṣa, according to the white dharma of passion and the white dharma of semen.

167. Then, having projected the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) of wisdom (*prajñā*), one should request initiation with the mantra syllables. Having visualized the deities mentioned by those respective mantra syllables as being present before one and having worshipped them, likewise recite here: "Oṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ huṃ hūṃ lūṃ haḷ oṃ ā ī ṝ ū ḷ! May the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, with vases of vajra-amṛta, initiate me; svāhā!"

OṂ AṂ Ī Ṛ UṂ LŪṂ! May all the Buddhas bind upon me the vajra crown consisting of the five Buddhas; HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ! OṂ Ā Ā ĀṂ ĀḤ HA HĀ HAṂ HAḤ PHREṂ HOḤ! May all the Pāramitās bind upon me the vajra ribbon; HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ! OṂ HŪṂ HOḤ! O Vajra and Vajra-bell, whose nature is consciousness and gnosis, and which consist of compassion and wisdom—may Vajrasattva together with his consort bestow you upon my right and left hands; HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ!

Oṃ a ā e ai ar ār o au al ālū aṃ aḥ! May all the Bodhisattvas together with their consorts, at all times, grant me the vajra vow of enjoying all desires; svāhā! Oṃ ha hā ya yā rarāva vā la lā! May all the Kings of Wrath together with their consorts grant me the name preceded by the vajra of the nature of universal equanimity—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!

Having made this supplication: *Oṃ vaṃ! May the Lord of the Maṇḍala, Wisdom and Means marked by the lotus and vajra, grant me the limb of the gnosis of vajra-bliss! Haṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!*—one should then visualize oneself as consecrated by the seven consecrations.
Thereafter, one should maintain the pride of having obtained the seven consecrations, thinking:
*Oṃ, I am one who has attained the seven stages through the seven consecrations of all the Tathāgatas!* This is the procedure for the authorization of the seven consecrations.
Thus is the accomplishment of speech; this is the *karmarājāgrī* samādhi, which is the limb of the *upasādhana*.

Then, furthermore, in that regard—the practitioner (*mantrī*) should request the higher consecrations, beginning with the vase, with these mantra-words: *oṃ oṃ prajñopāyau viśvamātarau kalaśābhiṣekaṃ me dadatāṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ āḥ prajñopāyau guhyābhiṣekaṃ me dadatāṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
"Oṃ hūṃ! May Wisdom and Means, the Vajrasattva and Viśvamātṛ, grant me the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka) phaṭ!
Having thus supplicated, one should visualize oneself as having been initiated according to the procedure to be described below, and then assume the divine pride (ahaṃkāra).

One should cultivate the sense of self-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) as follows: "Oṃ oṃ! I have been consecrated by Vajrasattva with the vajra-vase consecration; I am the son of Vajrasattva, having attained the stage (*bhūmi*) of Acalā. "Oṃ ā! I have been consecrated by Vajrasattva with the secret consecration; I am the crown prince (*yuvarāja*) of Vajrasattva, having attained the ninth stage. "Oṃ hūṃ! I have been consecrated by Vajrasattva with the consecration of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*); I am the second Vajradhara, having attained the stage of Dharmameghā."
Thus concludes the ritual for the higher consecration (168).
Thereafter, one should request the fourth consecration, which is higher than the higher, with this mantra:
OṂ HOḤ PRAJÑOPĀYĀTMAKAVAJRASATTVA MAHĀMUDRĀJÑĀNĀBHISHEKAṂ ME PRAYACCHA OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ HOḤ PHAṬ.
Then, having requested [the initiation], one should meditate upon oneself as being consecrated by means of stainlessness;
thereafter, one should assume the identity of Vajrasattva:

"Oṃ Hoḥ! Consecrated by the fourth initiation of the syllable of the Dharmadhātu, I am myself Vajrasattva, the second [Buddha], who has attained the twelfth stage, the Great Being Vajrasattva, the Supreme Syllable, the Lord Kālacakra, the Victor over the Three Worlds, the embodiment of the syllable E-Vaṃ. This is the procedure for the higher initiation.

Likewise, in the glorious *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, the venerable Mañjuśrīpāda has spoken regarding the meaning of consecration: "The touching of the breasts of the Wisdom Consort, the supreme tasting of nectar, and the embrace; the fourth moment occurring during union with the Wisdom Consort when the bodhicitta has melted into nectar—all that is indeed mundane, shown for the sake of the path through supreme compassion. The supramundane consecration is that which consists of the attachment to the divine mudrā of the Supreme Lord of Jinas."
Thus, in this context, one should meditate upon the yoga of Caṇḍālī;

and so it is said in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "In all cases here within the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), the perfection of the body is the Supreme King of the Mandala (*maṇḍalarājāgrī*); the perfection of speech is the Supreme King of Action (*karmarājāgrī*) because of the initiation of the activities of the action-faculties; the perfection of the drops of the bodhicitta is the Yoga of the Drop (*binduyoga*);
and the attainment of bliss from the emission of the semen is the Subtle Yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*)."
And that [attainment] occurs for men at the end of sixteen years;

therefore, for its utilization, the teacher should perform the rites of marriage, taking of the hand, and so forth, as well as the transmission of wisdom (*prajñā*) to the disciple. By means of that [wisdom], the method for achieving his bliss is taught: by the *karmamudrā* for the immature, by the *jñānamudrā* for the middling, and by the *mahāmudrā* for the supreme yogins.

Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "One should first thoroughly train a girl of sixteen years, of noble family, adorned with beauty and youth; having consecrated her, one should begin the practice."
One should place the passion-elements of body, speech, and mind at the forehead and other locations; then, with "svāhā," one should purify the lotus at the secret place and the great uṣṇīṣa.
By means of the syllable ĀḤ, there is an eight-petaled lotus, and by means of the syllable HŪṂ, it is endowed with a vajra;
thus, the lotus together with the vajra exists due to the cause of the movement of wisdom (prajñā).
The ritual procedure for the sādhana of the Blessed Śrī Kālacakra:
one should visualize one's own vajra as five-pronged by means of the syllable HŪṂ;
in its center, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus by means of the syllable ĀḤ.
Having thus formed the lotus and the vajra,
the yogi, uttering "HŪṂ PHAṬ" and maintaining the pride of Vajradhara, should place [the vajra] within the lotus; having established the linga in the bhaga, he must not emit the bodhicitta.
One should meditate upon the form of the Buddha as the entirety of the three realms without exception.
The Caṇḍālī, ignited at the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas;
Locanā and the others, such as the eyes, are burned, and once they are consumed, the Moon flows forth.

Amṛta flows in the form of drops in the form of semen; this is known as the Binduyoga. Holding the half of the half of the sixteen drops, he is partless (akala), beyond all calculation, and the holder of the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna.
Known as the subtle yoga, it proceeds upward from the [four] outflows and so forth;
this Śaṅkhinī is the Mahāmudrā and is celebrated as Caṇḍālī.
That which is above the navel is Ḍombinī, while Avadhūtī is the nose of man.
The vital breath consists of five rays and carries the five mandalas;
it is known as a mustard seed at the tip of the nose, and that is remembered as prāṇāyāma.
It is the thorough knowledge of the three worlds and of the elements without exception.
When the vital breath is restrained, that [universe] consisting of the moving and the non-moving is within the mustard seed;
in the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is the characteristic of emptiness in space,
where the mind is fixed upon the nose and its region.
"But at the end of the sign, on that line, the yogi should contemplate the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings; and therein [he performs] meditation and so forth.

Here, however, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), the emanation of the form of the mandala circle within the yoga of the deity during the contemplation of the moving and non-moving world refers to the emanation of sons and daughters from the *bodhicitta* for those in cyclic existence.
Thus, for those born from a womb, the perfection of body, speech, mind, and gnosis occurs by the limit of sixteen years;

for deities, it is through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); and for Buddhas, it is through the power of the four liberations (*vimokṣa*). This is according to the conventional and ultimate truths.

Furthermore, in that same context, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), there is again the rule: "At the tip of the nose in the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), [one visualizes] a mustard seed and so forth."

In this context, at the time of assuming the pride (*garvavahana*) of Vajradhara, one should cultivate the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) thinking: "I am of the nature of the wheel (*cakra*) of the passion for the worship of gnosis (*jñānapūjānurāgaṇa*).

Furthermore, in that regard, up until the age of sixteen, there is the passion for the worship of gnosis; at that time, one should say, "I am of the nature of that. This is the rule for the Blessed One here in the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*).
Moreover, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) has been briefly indicated here as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The specific details of the practice have not been written here for fear of excessive length;
one should recite the mantra, and as it is said therein: "by means of mantra-recitation and so forth."
Here, what is called "mantra-recitation" (japa) is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa-saṃyama);

by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the yoga of exhalation, inhalation, and retention (recaka-pūraka-kumbhaka) is included. Constant service through this [yoga] causes the deities to become granters of boons; it is not [achieved] by unrestrained breath or by mere verbal chatter—this is the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
According to the interpretable meaning (neyārtha), however, recitation with a rosary and so forth should be performed for the sake of ordinary accomplishments (sāmānya-siddhi).
Then, by resorting to the rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), one should recite the mantra with a rosary made of pearls or crystal.
In this regard, the six-limbed mantra of the Blessed One is:
*oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ haḥ svāhā*. This same mantra, ending with "namas," is used for the rite of pacification.
In that manner, one should perform the dismissal of the deities;

and as it is said therein: "Having meditated here upon the King of Mandalas, the Supreme King of Rituals, the yoga of the drop (*bindu*), and the subtle yoga, and having performed worship and praise with the verse beginning 'Homage to you, O supreme Vajra-granter of boons,' and so forth, then for the sake of dismissing the deities of the mandala, one should meditate on the fivefold vajra within the uṣṇīṣa."
One should emanate the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) upon its central hub (*varaṭaka*).
Then, having meditated on a vajra with a single prong in the heart—the wheel of phenomena (*dharmacakra*)—one should emanate [the deities] such as Dhūmā.
Next, having meditated on a vajra with seventeen prongs in the forehead—the wheel of co-emergence (*sahajacakra*)—one should emanate the deities of the aggregates and elements upon its central hub.
Then, having meditated upon a thirty-three-pronged vajra at the throat in the sambhogacakra, one should dismiss the twelve sense bases and the four wrathful deities from its central hub (*varaṭaka*).

Then, having meditated upon a sixty-five-pronged vajra at the navel in the nirmāṇacakra according to the procedure for the sādhana of the Blessed One Śrī Kālacakra, one should dismiss the deities such as Cāmuṇḍā and Bhīmā from its central hub. Then, having meditated upon a thirty-three-pronged vajra at the secret place, one should dismiss the deities such as Mārīcī from its central hub.

In this manner, having visualized thirty-one prongs of vajras at the locations mentioned in the verses of homage within the *karmacakra*s for the twelve deities beginning with Viṣṇu together with their retinues, one should dismiss them into their respective central hubs (*varaṭaka*).
Likewise, having visualized seven-pronged vajras in the *kriyācakra*s for the deities beginning with Nāga and Śvānāsya, one should dismiss them into their respective central hubs.

Now, if some person of duller faculties is unable to perform the meditation on the maṇḍala circle consisting of the three circles of mind, speech, and body as described above, such a person should meditate solely upon the mind-maṇḍala characterized as previously stated.

And so it is said there: "Having dismissed the eight goddesses beginning with Dhūmā, and having placed the eight jars, the conch, and so forth, upon the lotus of the Lord of Jinas, sometimes the Śrī-cakra—the mind-maṇḍala consisting of twenty-five principles—comes to be in the center of the womb, O King. Even when seated, the Blessed One then becomes like the Śrī-samāja;
there is no fault here because of the absence of a [material] substrate.

Knowing this, practitioners should meditate upon this Blessed One within their own minds as Power (śakti). Or, for the sake of initiation, there may be a maṇḍala devoid of the external wheel, according to the family (kula)."

In this case as well, one should meditate upon everything from the previously mentioned purification of body, speech, and mind up to the dismissal of the deities; then, having formed the ego-identification with "Oṃ, I am Vajrasattva, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, the tamer of the difficult-to-tame, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ," one should offer the bali. And so it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*: "Having performed the dismissal in this manner, one should offer the bali at the three junctions of the day."
Then, having purified the substances of the previously mentioned pledge (*samaya*) and having gratified the host of deities, one should offer the *bali*.

And so it is said therein: "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Hoḥ! Having first purified the liquor here according to the sequence, one should always awaken it; having ignited it and visualized it as the molten moon, one should gradually take a drop from that vessel with the tip of the ring finger—which is like a lotus with rays of the moon—and placing it on the ground outside, one should draw a triangle resembling the sun and a circle in its center."

In the midst of that, having meditated upon the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) which encompasses even the three realms of existence, that mantra-practitioner performs the libation and other rites daily with his thumb and ring finger. First, he offers a bali-oblation here for the lords of regions and villages, using their names at the beginning, middle, and end. Furthermore, the practitioner gives two morsels to Hārītī, and another bali-oblation to the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*). He gives the first portion of the food to the messengers (*dūtī*) in the dwelling on the surface of the earth with the mantras of the Lords, and the remains of what has been eaten to the spirits (*bhūta*). Then he recites this auspicious verse of giving: [The verse follows] *Note: The verse is not provided in the source text.*

One should perform the *aṅganyāsa* with one's own vajras upon the head, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and crown. At the time of sleep, during worship, and during sexual union, one should perform the *aṅga* and *vaktra* [nyāsas] according to the respective families. Thereafter, upon a tripod arisen from the letter *A*, there are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*), produced from the seed-syllables of the aggregates and elements situated within a skull-cup arisen from the syllable *Oṃ*. These are melted by the fire ignited by the wind-mandala situated below, stirred by the vajra born from the syllable *Hūṃ*, and become of one flavor (*samarasa*) with that very [vajra] in the form of a lunar liquid. To purify these, there are the mantra words as follows:

And likewise, in the *Śrīvimalaprabhā*: "One should offer a bali-oblation to the lord of the eastern region and village, having purified [the area] with these mantra-words: *oṃ oṃ vajracandra sarvadharma-viśuddhasvabhāva sarvadharmān viśodhaya svāhā;
oṃ āḥ vajrasūrya sarvadharmaprabodhaka sarvadharmān prabodhaya svāhā;
oṃ hūṃ vajrānala sarvadharmapradīpaka sarvadharmān pradīpaya svāhā*."
Oṃ hoḥ! O you who make all phenomena into vajra-nectar, make all phenomena into vajra-nectar, svāhā!
With these mantra words, one should purify with the left hand in the proper sequence and awaken with the right.

Having touched [the substance] and covered it with joined palms, one should kindle it; having made it Vajrāmṛta with the Vajragaruḍa-mudrā, one should perform the invocation of the ruler of the region with the Trailokyavijaya-mudrā,

that of the lords of villages and places with the Śvāna-mudrā, that of the Krodharājas with the Pañcaśūka-mudrā, that of all [others] with the Kartṛ-mudrā, that of the gods with the Khaḍga-mudrā, that of the planets with the Ratna-mudrā, that of the nāgas with the Padma-mudrā, and that of the pretas with the Cakra-mudrā.

And likewise, it is stated there: having formed a hollowed cup with the hands, the two thumbs joined, the two little fingers joined and resembling lotus petals, the two middle fingers extended, the two index fingers bent at half-moon shape, the two ring fingers tucked beneath on the back of the middle fingers upon one's own palms—having thus bound the *pañcaśūka* mudrā; then, with the two little fingers joined to each other on the backs of the uneven palms, and the tips of the index, middle, ring, and thumb fingers joined together—this is the *garuḍa* mudrā.

By joining the backs of the hands in the fist-position, with the thumbs between the index fingers and the little fingers mutually bound together—this is the Trailokyavijaya-mudrā according to the *Śrī Kālacakra Bhagavat Sādhanavidhi*.
Then, from the right vajra-fist, one should slightly extend the four fingers beginning with the index finger; this is the Śvāna-mudrā (Dog-mudrā).
By binding the vajra-fist, with the little fingers in the shape of a half-moon, this is the Karti-mudrā (Scissors-mudrā).

The *khaḍgamudrā* (sword mudrā) is formed by pressing the thumb with the little finger and the ring finger, while the index and middle fingers are held straight like arrows. The *ratnamudrā* (jewel mudrā) is formed by placing the middle finger in the center of the five fingers with the palms facing upward. The *padmamudrā* (lotus mudrā) is formed by spreading the index and other fingers like a four-petaled lotus, with the thumb and little finger [held inward]. The *cakramudrā* (wheel mudrā) is formed by extending the fingers from the hollowed palms of both hands.
Thus is the description of the mudrās.

Then, "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, [Name], come quickly! Accept this bali offering; having eaten and drunk, and having attained satisfaction, bring peace to all sentient beings and go, go to your own place, svāhā!"—this is the mantra for the bali offering for the ruler of a country and the ruler of a village.

In each case, if the name of the region or the village consists of three, five, or seven syllables, one should offer the *bali* by means of the designation of the initial, middle, and final syllables;
however, if the name consists of two, four, six, or an even number of syllables, one should offer it by means of the designation of the initial and final syllables.
Then, having brought face-to-face the wrathful deities previously emanated, there are the mantra-words for the offering of the *bali*.

And so they say: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ! To Uṣṇīṣa, Sumbha, Niśumbha, Vighnāntaka, Nīladaṇḍa, Prajñāntaka, Ṭakkirāja, Padmāntaka, Acala, Yamāntaka, Mahābala, together with their retinues—we offer this bali, perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, and unbroken grain. May they come with their retinues and quickly accept, eat, and drink this bali: jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Being fully satisfied, may they grant peace, nourishment, protection, shelter, and guardianship to all sentient beings! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Vajradhara commands: svāhā!
Thus is the *bali* mantra for all the wrathful deities (*krodha*).

Next are the *bali* mantra words for the perfected ones of space and so forth (*ākāśādikṛtsnasiddha*): Oṃ ā hūṃ hāṃ: To those accomplished in space, wind, fire, water, and earth, together with their retinues, we offer this *bali*, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains. May they come with their retinues and quickly accept, eat, and drink this *bali*. Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Being fully satisfied, may they grant peace, nourishment, protection, defense, and concealment to all sentient beings. Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Vajradhara commands it. Svāhā!

Then, the mantra-words for the offering (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions: *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ! To Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Nairṛti, Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Samudra, Īśvara, Indra, and Yakṣa, together with their retinues, we offer this *bali*, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamp, and unbroken grains. May they come with their retinues and quickly accept, eat, and drink this *bali*. Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Being fully satisfied, may they perform peace, nourishment, protection, defense, and concealment for all sentient beings—*vi prabhā pṛ... vi prabhā pṛ...* Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Vajradhara commands: *svāhā*!"

Then, the mantra-words for the offering (bali) to the planets: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ ho! To Rāhu, Kālāgni, Candra, Sūrya, Budha, Maṅgala, Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Ketu, and Śani, together with your retinues, we offer this bali, perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, and unbroken rice. May you come with your retinues and quickly accept, eat, and drink this bali: jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Being fully satisfied, may you grant peace, nourishment, protection, shelter, and guardianship to all sentient beings! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Vajradhara commands: svāhā!

Then, the offering mantras for the *nāgas* are as follows: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ! To Jayavijaya, Padmakaṭaka, Vāsuki, Śaṅkhapāla, Kulika, Ananta, Takṣaka, Mahāpadma, and their retinues—we offer this *bali*, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains. May they come with their retinues and quickly accept, eat, and drink this *bali*. Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Being fully satisfied, may they grant peace, nourishment, protection, defense, and concealment to all sentient beings. Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Vajradhara commands it. Svāhā!

Then, the mantra syllables for the offering (*bali*) to the spirits (*bhūta*): Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ! To those with the faces of *vetāḍas*, distorted beings, dogs, crows, pigs, vultures, tigers, owls, jackals, and *garuḍas*, together with their retinues, we offer this *bali*, perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and unbroken rice. May they come with their retinues and quickly accept, eat, and drink this *bali*: jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Being fully satisfied, may they provide peace, nourishment, protection, defense, and concealment for all sentient beings! Huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Vajradhara commands it: svāhā!
Thus is the mantra for the *bhūta-bali*.
One should dismiss [the deities] in that manner; as it has been said: "At the time of dismissal, one should cause the *krodha*-cakra to enter the *guhya-cakra* at the syllable *hā~*;
[and] the *śūnyakṛtsna*-cakra and so forth into the *uṣṇīṣa* at the syllable *a~*."
One should cause the wheel of the world-protectors to enter the forehead at the letter *i*, the wheel of the planets at the throat at the letter *ṛ*,
the wheel of the nāgas at the heart at the letter *u*,
and the wheel of the spirits at the navel at the letter *lṛ*; this is the dismissal (*visarjana*).

O Śrī Lokanātha, that which was spoken by you has been extracted by me, a fool of dull intellect, for the sake of memory; O Protector, be gracious to me, and O you whose mind is moist with compassion, forgive me, O Father, just as one endures the fickleness of his own son.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the sādhana of the Blessed One Kālacakra, extracted from the Vimalaprabhā composed by the illustrious Puṇḍarīka, the emanation of Lokeśvara.
This work is by the great scholar Dharmākaraśāntipāda, whose lotus feet are honored by millions of kings, cowherds, and forest-dwellers.
May there be auspiciousness at all times!
